transcript:
Header: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood CSM), Liam O'Connor (Quantaco Head of ML), Sara Nguyen (Quantaco SRE), Diego Ramos (Quantaco Product), Priya Shah (Quantaco Infra)

Summary: quick cost/econ review of the pilot. Reviewed tokens/sec/$ baselines, KV/prefix caching impact, batching tradeoffs, and next steps to run dedicated pool runs. Some background noise, a couple of words auto-transcribed wrong (e.g., "K-V cache" as "KV case").

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep this tight — 45 minutes, cost/econ focus today. Ravi's got the numbers from last week's runs.
[00:18] Ravi: cool, hi all. Quick context, we ran three sets: hosted baseline (small batch, default runtime), hosted with prefix/KV caching enabled, and a dedicated GPU pool run with quantized model. I pulled the bench spreadsheet, link in chat — docs/benchmarks/quantaco-poc-costs.xlsx (shared).
[00:35] Liam: okay good thanks. can you start with the tokens/sec per dollar numbers? that's what the execs keep asking for.
[00:42] Ravi: sure. so first caveat, numbers are noisy — depends on prompt length distribution and hit rate for the cache. but rough ballpark: hosted baseline (no caching, batch size 1) gave us about 1,200 tokens/sec per dollar for the workload we sent — that's tokens/sec/$ as measured by average throughput divided by cost per second. When we turned on prefix/KV caching at session level with ~45% hit rate, effective tokens/sec/$ rose to ~3,900, so roughly a 3.2x improvement.
[01:12] Sara (interject): sorry just to clarify, is that tokens per dollar or tokens per second per dollar? the metric confused me in the spreadsheet.
[01:20] Ravi: yeah sorry, shorthand — we mean effective tokens served per dollar per second normalized; think of it as throughput per cost. in the sheet it's tokens_per_dollar which is total tokens generated over the run divided by total cost. the throughput p50/p95 numbers are separate.
[01:36] Diego: and what did the dedicated pool look like? we were hoping dedicated would give better economics.
[01:41] Ravi: dedicated helped on steady-state throughput. On the dedicated quantized run (8-bit), with batching tuned we saw tokens_per_dollar around 12,000 — that included larger batch sizes (8 and 16) and a higher cache hit rate because we enabled conversation-level prefix caching. So dedicated + quantization + caching is the best-case for cost. Caveat: p95 latency rose.
[02:05] Jordan: can you give the latency numbers? some of our product folks will freak if p95 goes above 300ms.
[02:10] Ravi: absolutely. hosted baseline (batch=1) p50 ~75ms, p95 ~210ms. Hosted with caching (same batch=1 but cache hits avoid recompute for prefixes) p50 ~60ms, p95 ~180ms. Dedicated, with batch=8, p50 ~110ms, p95 ~340ms. If we lower the batch to 4 on dedicated, p95 drops to ~260ms and tokens_per_dollar drops about 12%.
[02:40] Priya: so that's the classic latency vs cost tradeoff. do you have numbers for batch=16?
[02:45] Ravi: batch=16 improved tokens_per_dollar by another ~18% over batch=8 but p95 jumped to ~450ms which is probably outside your SLOs. Also warm-up for KV cache matters; cold-starts see lower hit rates for the first few requests.
[03:02] Liam: what's the delta for quantization? 8-bit vs 4-bit? we were considering 4-bit to save more.
[03:07] Ravi: 8-bit gave us about 2.1x cost reduction compared to fp16 baseline with negligible quality regressions on your eval sets (we ran 500 prompt checks). 4-bit gave roughly 3.8x improvement but we did see a couple of edge-case hallucinations and tokenization drift on some prompts — not huge but noticeable. We can A/B that on your prompts.
[03:34] Sara: how about cache hit rate improvements? you said 45% — can we get to 70%?
[03:38] Ravi: yes with two levers: persist session-level KV caches and increase prefix standardization. In the runs where we normalized prompts and stripped non-essential metadata we saw hit rates approach 68–72% and the tokens_per_dollar moved proportionally. So we recommend you provide canonical templates.
[03:58] Diego: any changes needed to our client? we're instrumenting prompts via the SDK now.
[04:02] Maya: minimal — use the conversation_id header and set the caching policy in the request to session. We have an SDK flag; Ravi can share a snippet.
[04:10] Ravi: yep I'll paste the snippet after. it's a one-line header and a small client-side normalization step.

[04:30] Speaker 1: (inaudible) did someone say model fallback?
[04:33] Ravi: yes — also worth mentioning smart routing: if the dedicated pool is saturated, we can fallback to a slightly cheaper hosted variant (smaller model or more quantized) — that keeps latency stable but shifts quality. We instrument that as a policy.
[04:50] Liam: how do we calculate cost for reserved vs on-demand dedicated?
[04:54] Maya: we provided two examples in the pricing sheet: monthly reserved for a dedicated pool (committed) gives you ~35–45% cheaper per-token vs on-demand dedicated; but you pay the commitment regardless of usage. For pilot it's common to start with a small reserved commit to lock better rate and then adjust after 30 days.
[05:12] Priya: security question — when you talk about caching, are prefixes stored encrypted, and can we use our KMS?
[05:18] Ravi: yes — prefix/KV caches are encrypted at rest and we support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM in Private deployments. For hosted, we offer envelope encryption; for Private you can bring your own key. We'll include the security doc.

[05:40] Sara: one more operational question — what does the trace look like when a cache miss forces recompute? i.e., how visible are the memcache hits in Redwood Console?
[05:48] Jordan: we surfaced cache hit/miss metrics per-route and per-session in Console — you get token-level breakdowns and you can filter by conversation_id. We can also add a synthetic test route to show expected hit rates.

[06:10] Ravi: back to numbers for a sec — in the dedicated runs we measured end-to-end tokens generated per $1: baseline (no cache, fp16) ~2.8M tokens/$, with 8-bit quant + caching ~11.9M tokens/$ on that workload. Again those scale with hit rate and prompt length. We added a sensitivity tab in the spreadsheet showing tokens_per_dollar at 30/45/70% cache hit.
[06:36] Diego: that sheet is super helpful. is the cost model including networking and storage?
[06:42] Maya: it includes compute cost (GPU), storage for model bits, and a conservative network egress estimate for cross-region. If you run fully in-province / VPC with no cross-region egress the network number is lower; we'll model that once we know your region.

[07:00] Liam: what's our recommended pilot config to show meaningful cost savings but stay within latency SLOs?
[07:05] Ravi: for your app (mostly short prompts with a few long ones), recommended pilot: Dedicated reserved small pool, model quantized to 8-bit, batching capped at 4 (to keep p95 < 300ms), and session prefix caching with prompt normalization. That gave us the ~2.8–3.5x improvement over hosted baseline in our runs without pushing p95 over 300ms.
[07:26] Sara: if we cap batches at 4, how much headroom do we have for load spikes?
[07:30] Ravi: we can configure burst capacity and autoscaling; small batches mean lower aggregation efficiency but you can autoscale to handle spikes. There's a tradeoff (cost vs headroom). We can simulate your QPS distribution in the next run.

[07:50] Maya: quick note on reporting — we'll send a version of that bench spreadsheet with a normalized "tokens_per_dollar" chart and a separate latency-vs-batch curve. Also include a cost sensitivity table for cache hit rates 30/45/70.
[08:05] Liam: perfect. any blockers from infra side? Priya?
[08:09] Priya: KMS and VPC peering — we need to confirm the peering CIDR and KMS policies; otherwise sounds fine. We'll share the infra ticket by Friday.

[08:20] Ravi: small gotcha — when you're instrumenting client-side normalization, watch out for user-specific metadata embedded in prompts (timestamps, uuids). those kill cache hit rates. We recommend a small canonicalization lib; we'll share ours.

[08:40] Maya: ok let's do a quick recap and owners.
[08:44] Maya: Ravi to run dedicated + batch experiments (1/4/8/16) with KV cache toggled and share p50/p95 and tokens_per_dollar (due 2026-03-06).
[08:54] Maya: Maya to send pricing + pilot SOW + bench spreadsheet link (due 2026-03-05).
[08:59] Maya: Quantaco (Liam) to share canonical prompts and seq-length distro (due 2026-03-05).

[09:08] Diego: minor note — we'll also run an internal eval to check quality at 4-bit if you want us to; should we share the eval harness?
[09:14] Ravi: yes please — if you can share the harness we can run a 4-bit vs 8-bit quality comparison on your data. that'll help decide.

[09:24] Speaker 2: (overlap) one last question — do you anticipate model rollout risk? e.g., if we roll a quantized model and see regression, can we fallback?
[09:31] Maya: yes, rollouts and automatic fallback are part of Redwood — canary or A/B and auto-fallback to previous variant. We'll show the rollout policy in the deep dive.

[09:44] Liam: great. thanks everyone. that was actionable.

[09:50] End: quick post-call notes: Jordan will add a Console demo slot to next week's deep dive. Ravi will upload the raw bench outputs to the sheet. Maya will share the pricing and SOW.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hears of product names (e.g., "KV cache" -> "KV case"), speaker attribution glitches at 04:30 and 09:24.
